 ‘GTA 6’ Rejected Hollywood. ‘Red Dead Redemption’ is in Play — for $100M+
 Scoop: One of Rockstar Games’ biggest titles could see an adaptation after years of the company refusing to engage 
 By
 Lesley Goldberg 
 Nov 18, 2026

 I wrote about the DC Studios coup , scooped Adults ’ season three renewal in conversation with John Landgraf, and wrote about the sleight of hand behind HBO’s buying spree . I’m lesley.goldberg@theankler.com 
 It’s the ultimate flex:  Rockstar Games, the Take-Two subsidiary behind  Grand Theft Auto , doesn’t need Hollywood. And despite years of incoming calls from entertainment companies eager to adapt the blockbuster 30-year franchise, Rockstar still isn’t interested, multiple sources tell me.
 But I can exclusively reveal that another of Rockstar’s multibillion-dollar franchises may be in play. Sources tell me the company is more open to bringing  Red Dead Redemption , its wildly popular Western action-adventure franchise, to film or television. 
 The potential price tag? “At one point, they were throwing around a purchase price of more than $100 million minimum for licensing rights,” says an agent who works with writers in the video game space. For perspective, Amazon paid $250 million in 2017 for the global television rights to  The Lord of the Rings .
 Rockstar Games did not immediately respond to request for comment.
 The revelation comes as Rockstar prepares to unleash  Grand Theft Auto 6  on Thursday, ending an unprecedented 13-year wait. With rave reviews already landing, the game is expected to trigger a global case of “GTA Flu” as millions of fans disappear into their consoles — and generate an astonishing $3 billion to $5 billion in its first week alone. (It’s ultimately expected to make three to four times GTA 5 — $1.15 billion.) 
 Those numbers help explain why the balance of power between Hollywood and the video game industry has shifted so dramatically. With a global gaming market valued at well over $200 billion and 3.7 billion active players, Hollywood increasingly needs gaming’s biggest franchises more than gaming needs Hollywood.
 And Hollywood is willing to pay.
 Even as streamers cut back on original programming and rein in budgets, Amazon, Netflix and FX are spending $15 million to $25 million per episode on adaptations of  Tomb Raider ,  Assassin’s Creed  and  Far Cry , hoping to convert legions of gamers into old-fashioned TV viewers. The success of Amazon’s Fallout  and HBO’s  The Last of Us  has only intensified the pursuit.
 But these are expensive bets, and not every gaming giant wants to play Hollywood’s game.
 Today, I’ve got new reporting on where the biggest streamers are placing their bets, which adaptations are already running into trouble and why some of the most valuable franchises in entertainment remain tantalizingly out of reach.
